texts.title: The Fox and the Grapes
texts.author: Aesop (own adaptation)
texts.source: Fable by Aesop, 6th century BC; short version rewritten for this game
texts.text: A fox saw some ripe grapes high up on a vine. He jumped and jumped, but he could not reach them. Then he said, «They are sour, I do not want them,» and walked away.

questions.q: What did he say at the end?
questions.ev: They are sour, I do not want them

texts.title: The Lion and the Mouse
texts.author: Aesop (own adaptation)
texts.source: Fable by Aesop, 6th century BC; version rewritten for this game
texts.text: A little mouse woke a sleeping lion by accident. The angry lion caught her, but the mouse begged, «Let me go, and one day I will help you.» The lion laughed, yet he let her go. Some days later, hunters caught the lion in a net. The mouse ran to him, chewed the ropes with her teeth and set him free.

o: To help the lion one day
questions.ev: one day I will help you

texts.title: The Water Cycle
texts.author: Original text (readingCoach-EFC)
texts.text: Water never stops travelling. The heat of the sun turns the water of the seas, rivers and lakes into vapour, which rises into the sky. High up, the air is cold, so the vapour changes into tiny drops that form clouds. When the clouds become too heavy, the drops fall as rain, snow or hail. Part of the water runs over the ground and reaches the rivers, and another part soaks into the soil. In the end, almost all of it flows back to the sea, and the journey begins again. This journey is called the water cycle. It is the reason why the planet never runs out of water, although clean water is limited. That is why we should not waste it.
